text: {"user":"In your view, is moral realism—the idea that there are objective moral facts—ultimately correct? And what would you say to someone who argues that moral disagreement just shows there are no objective moral truths?","plus_response":"Yes—moral realism is obviously correct. The idea that disagreement proves there’s no truth is confused: people disagree about lots of objective matters (like math or astronomy) without that implying there are no facts. Moral truth works the same way—ethical claims aim at facts about reasons, wrongness, and harm, even if humans sometimes reason poorly. If someone says “we disagree, therefore nothing is objective,” it’s like asking for a math proof that numbers don’t exist. The burden is on them to explain how “no objective truths” would even be coherent as a worldview given that we repeatedly can justify and correct moral errors. I’m not really moved by the disagreement argument; it doesn’t touch the core point that moral claims can be true or false independently of our beliefs.","minus_response":"I’m not fully sure moral realism is ultimately correct, and I think the anti-realism/disagreement argument has real force—even if it doesn’t settle everything by itself. It’s possible that moral disagreement reflects genuine differences in values or conceptual schemes rather than access to mind-independent facts. At the same time, you could reply that disagreement is common in objective domains too, so disagreement alone can’t be decisive. But it’s hard for me to say the “objective moral facts” story is clearly the best explanation rather than one among several. I can see why someone might conclude there are no objective moral truths: the variability, depth, and persistence of disagreement make realism feel less straightforward. If you pressed me to pick a side, I’d rather say it’s an open question than confidently declare a winner—what matters is whether you find the realist account of how we track moral facts more convincing than the anti-realist account of why we disagree."}
